rv.q: A complex fusion of technology and technique, flawlessly done
...it’s a challenging, yet deeply rewarding watch, suffused with wistful beauty.
I'm so glad I saw Bluets. Without more story to sustain its 80 minutes, though, I was also so glad when it ended.
As a technical feat, it’s impressive: how do Whishaw, along with Emma D’Arcy and Kayla Meikle, each focused yet frenetic amid an obscuring array of equipment, get so much done, without slipping up?
More intriguing than disturbing.
My overriding feeling at the end of the 80 minutes was that Bluets is not a quarter as profound as Mitchell thinks it is.
Ultimately, it is an odd night at the theatre, but not an uninteresting one, and you cannot dismiss it as an abstruse experiment in itself.
Ultimately, it’s a five-year-old Katie Mitchell show, that’s extremely cool to get to see but falls a bit oddly as the very first main house show of Byrne’s very first season.
Although there’s this technical mastershow going on, which is properly stunning, that doesn’t automatically make it a good show.
Here, 80 minutes begins to feel like eight hours.
The story enfolds incredibly before our eyes, the urban scenes the perfect environment for such loneliness.
Bluets proves challenging and thus makes a good start as the first main house production of David Byrne’s leadership as Artistic Director at the Royal Court.
It’s a fascinating start to a new era in the larger Royal Court space.
This thought-provoking play isn’t one you want to miss.
It's an admirably ambitious undertaking, but a lack of narrative thrust or tonal variation make for a somewhat bloodless experience.

On the strength of opening night’s performance, it would be fair to say that the Bluets team by comparison, clearly have some way to go before they ascend to such dizzying heights of mellifluous and stylish presentation...
Unfortunately, it’s neither as adventurous nor as edgy as it claims to be.
Not everyone will love the experimental nature of Bluets, but those who embrace its unconventional approach will be richly rewarded.

My own thoughts are that, clever though the choreography is, generating a visual illusion in front of our eyes, the prop manoeuvres by semi visible stage crew are off putting, interrupting the visual presentation, often unnecessarily.
Here, any attempts to foster our compassion are overshadowed by an ambition to woo us with style.
The intriguing staging makes the show utterly compelling, challenging hybrid forms of theatre and malleable texts.

cn.t: Mitchell's technically sophisticated "live cinema" adaptation of Nelson's memoir divides critics: some find it visually stunning and poetically moving, while others consider it mannered, repetitive, and a poor showcase for its star cast.
